issues.legal_issue: A co-heir’s right to partition and a share in inherited property is not extinguished by adverse possession merely because another co-heir has possessed the property exclusively, profits were not shared, or a partition notice was left unpursued, without proof of a hostile denial of rights brought to the excluded co-heir’s knowledge for the statutory period.
material_facts: The claimant was established to be the deceased owner’s legally married second wife, and the owner died intestate, leaving her and two sons as heirs.
The courts found that the disputed B-schedule properties were the deceased owner’s self-acquired properties; the daughter had given up her share.
The claimant initially received income from the properties, but the sons later stopped paying her income and dealt with the properties.
The defendants relied on an alleged partition notice from 1955 that was not pursued; the claimant denied sending it, and the defendants did not produce the alleged advocate to prove it.
The claimant learned that properties were being sold and brought the partition suit in 1979.
The defendants did not establish a hostile, open denial of the claimant’s rights that had been brought home to her for the statutory period.
issues.conclusion: The claimant’s share was not extinguished by adverse possession. She was entitled to a one-third share in the B-schedule properties and rendition of accounts, and she was also entitled to her share in the A-schedule properties.
issues.legal_principle: Possession by one co-sharer is ordinarily possession for all co-sharers. Exclusive or long possession, or non-participation in profits, does not by itself establish ouster or adverse possession; there must be a hostile, open denial or repudiation of the other co-sharer’s rights brought to that co-sharer’s knowledge for the statutory period. A partition notice left unpursued is not, by itself, enough to extinguish the claimant’s rights. The Court relied on Hardit Singh v. Gurmukh Singh, AIR 1918 PC 1; Varada Pillai v. Jeevarathnammal; Mohaideen Abdul Kadir v. Mohammad Mahaideen Umma; Vidya Devi v. Prem Prakash, (1995) 4 SCC 496; Mohammad Baqar v. Naim-un-Nisa Bibi, AIR 1956 SC 548; Md. Mohammad Ali v. Jagadish Kalita, (2004) 1 SCC 271; T.P.R. Palania Pillai v. Amjath Ibrahim Rowther, AIR 1942 Madras 622; and Nirmal Chandra Das v. Mohitosh Das, AIR 1936 Calcutta 106. No statutory provision was cited in the judgment.

rule.if: partition_and_separate_possession_suit and claimant_is_coheir and property_possessed_by_coheirs and partition_notice_left_unpursued and clear_hostile_ouster_not_proved

predicates.partition_and_separate_possession_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking partition and separate possession of inherited property.
predicates.claimant_is_coheir: The person claiming partition is an heir who holds a share in the property with the other heirs.
predicates.property_possessed_by_coheirs: The other heirs possess or deal with the property as co-heirs.
predicates.partition_notice_left_unpursued: The claimant sent or was alleged to have sent a partition notice but did not pursue it at that time.
predicates.clear_hostile_ouster_not_proved: The other heirs did not prove a hostile and open denial of the claimant’s rights brought to the claimant’s knowledge for the statutory period.

issues.definition: When a co-heir seeks partition, possession by other co-heirs and an unpursued partition notice do not extinguish the claimant’s share if a qualifying hostile ouster has not been proved.
